nameStory: The "tasteless" part of this plant's name comes from its bland flavor, which sets it apart from its spicy cousin, biting stonecrop. Both plants are called "stonecrop" because they seem to grow right out of stone, thriving in rocky crevices and thin soils where other plants would struggle. The scientific name "sexangulare" means "six-angled," referring to the plant's distinctive spiraling pattern of six rows of leaves around each stem.
description: Tasteless stonecrop is a low-growing succulent that forms dense, carpet-like mats of fleshy green foliage. This hardy little plant reaches only about 5-6 inches tall but can spread widely across rocky surfaces and thin soils. Its thick, waxy leaves store water like tiny batteries, helping it survive in harsh conditions where most plants would wither. In early summer, it produces cheerful clusters of bright yellow, star-shaped flowers that buzz with visiting bees.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, thick, needle-like leaves arranged in six distinct spiraling rows around the stem - count them and you'll see the pattern! The leaves feel firm and waxy, like little green crayons, and taste completely bland if you nibble one.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with five pointed petals arranged in a perfect star shape, blooming in dense, flat-topped clusters during June and July. Each flower is small but numerous, creating a brilliant yellow carpet effect.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, dense mats that hug the ground and spread outward, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height. The stems creep along the surface, rooting as they go and creating thick carpets of succulent foliage.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves and stems feel thick, smooth, and waxy to the touch - like touching a well-made candle. The plant has a substantial, almost rubbery feel that's quite different from typical thin-leaved plants.

habitat: Look for tasteless stonecrop in sunny, well-drained spots with sandy or rocky soil throughout New England. It thrives in challenging locations like rock gardens, stone walls, gravelly roadsides, and thin soils where most plants struggle. This tough little succulent particularly loves south-facing slopes and areas with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green tips emerging from overwintered stems. The distinctive six-spiral leaf pattern becomes most obvious as stems actively grow.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with brilliant yellow star-shaped flowers blooming from June through July. The thick, waxy leaves are at their most prominent and the plant forms dense, spreading mats.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but the evergreen foliage remains thick and green. Plants may take on slightly reddish tints in exposed locations as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Stays evergreen in protected spots, though leaves may turn reddish-bronze in harsh conditions. The thick, succulent stems and six-spiral leaf arrangement remain visible for winter identification.

funFact: This little plant is basically a living roof tile - it's so good at surviving harsh conditions that it's commonly planted on green roofs in Europe, where it helps insulate buildings while requiring virtually no maintenance or watering!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with biting stonecrop, which looks nearly identical but has a sharp, peppery taste when you nibble a leaf - hence the name "tasteless" versus "biting." Remember: if it makes your mouth tingle, it's biting stonecrop; if it tastes like nothing, you've found tasteless stonecrop!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "tasteless," don't make this plant a regular snack - while not toxic, stonecrops can cause stomach upset in large quantities. The plant is native to Europe and Asia but has naturalized in parts of New England, often escaping from rock gardens where it's planted as an ornamental.
compareHints: Tasteless stonecrop's six-spiral leaf arrangement sets it apart from most other stonecrops in New England. Biting stonecrop looks nearly identical but has a sharp, peppery taste, while stringy stonecrop has longer, more loosely arranged leaves. The dense, short leaves and distinctive spiraling pattern make tasteless stonecrop unique among our regional stonecrops.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike biting stonecrop which has tiny needle-like leaves that taste peppery, stringy stonecrop has larger, flatter leaves in groups of three that are essentially tasteless.
Among New England stonecrops, biting stonecrop has the smallest, most tightly overlapping leaves and the most intense golden-yellow flowers.
Among New England's stonecrops, white stonecrop stands out for its pure white flowers and cylindrical leaves that look like tiny green hot dogs.
Woodland stonecrop stands out from its stonecrop relatives by its preference for shade and its unique four-petaled white flowers – most other Sedum species have five yellow petals and love full sun.
Among New England's stonecrops, Spanish stonecrop is distinguished by its particularly dense, mat-forming growth and tendency toward reddish stem coloration.

Mexican Stonecrop stands out from other New England stonecrops by its bright yellow-green 'lemon coral' coloration, while Stringy Stonecrop is more blue-green and Biting Stonecrop has shorter, more tightly packed triangular leaves.

Unlike the common yellow-flowered biting stonecrop or the shade-loving woodland stonecrop with its distinctive three-leaf clusters, cliff stonecrop has pure white flowers and distinctly blue-green (glaucous) leaves.
Unlike the yellow-flowered biting stonecrop with its pointed, cone-shaped leaves, thick-leaved stonecrop has white or pink flowers and much plumper, rounder leaves.
Makino's stonecrop differs from Stringy Stonecrop by its more compact, less trailing growth habit and smaller stature.
